# VG Cluster Signing Key

## Overview

A VG cluster that resolves runtime resources against a linked Cognigy.AI cluster
has to prove which VG cluster it is. It does so with a short-lived ES256 JWT,
signed by `vg-resource-resolver` with this cluster's private key and verified by
the AI cluster's `vg-runtime-api` against the public key that `api-server`
publishes at `/.well-known/jwks.json`.

Design: `vg-resources`
`docs/tdd/06-vg-in-ai/019-vg-resolver-runtime-api-jwt-keypair-auth-proposal.md`.

```
vg-resource-resolver ──signs JWT──▶ vg-runtime-api        (per call, VG ▶ AI)
      signing-key.pem                      │
                                           │ fetched on a timer, never per request
api-server /.well-known/jwks.json ◀────────┘              (AI ▶ VG)
    signing-key.pub.pem
```

One keypair per VG cluster, shared by every AI cluster it is linked to. There is
no per-link secret to provision.

## Secret Structure

One Secret holds both halves. Each pod mounts only the half it needs — the
`items:` selector in the volume is what makes that true, not a convenience.

| Key | Mounted into | Mode | Purpose |
|-----|--------------|------|---------|
| `signing-key.pem` | `vg-resource-resolver` | `0400` | Private key. Signs the per-call JWT. |
| `signing-key.pub.pem` | `api-server` | `0644` | Public key. Published as JWKS for AI clusters to verify against. |

Both filenames come from `vgCluster.signingKey.privateKeyFile` /
`publicKeyFile`; the generator writes whatever those say, so the mounts and the
Secret cannot disagree.

**What `items:` does and does not buy you.** It is *mount-time isolation*: a
compromise of `api-server` does not expose the signing key, because that pod
never receives it. It is **not** an RBAC boundary — both halves live in one
Secret, so anyone who can `get secret vg-cluster-signing-key` in the namespace
reads both regardless of what is mounted where. Two Secrets bound to two
ServiceAccounts would be the stronger control; that is not what this is.

The private half is mounted `0400`, tighter than the `0644` this chart uses for
the drachtio TLS key, so nothing else that lands in the resolver pod — an
ephemeral debug container, an injected sidecar — can read it. That works because
the resolver image declares no `USER` and runs as uid 0. **If you set
`resourceResolver.podSecurityContext.runAsUser`, set `fsGroup` to match**:
kubelet owns Secret volumes `root:fsGroup`, and without one a non-root process
cannot read the file at any mode tighter than `0644`.

The chart creates this Secret for you (see below) but offers no inline-PEM value,
on purpose: an inline value would put a private signing key in plaintext in a
values file that lives in a git repo. Helm's `randAlphaNum` cannot produce an EC
keypair either, which is why a hook Job does it rather than a template.

## The keypair is generated for you

**Nothing to do.** `vgCluster.signingKey.autoGenerate` defaults to `true`, and a
`pre-install,pre-upgrade` hook Job
(`templates/common-secrets/vg-cluster-signing-key-job.yaml`) creates the
`vg-cluster-signing-key` Secret on the cluster's next upgrade. Doing this by hand
across the fleet would be a lot of error-prone manual work; this is the same
approach `cognigy-ai-app` already uses for the platform's own auth-gateway
keypair.

Three properties worth knowing, because they are what make it safe:

- **It never regenerates.** If the Secret exists, the Job exits without touching
  it. A rotation is the sequenced operation below, never a side effect of
  `helm upgrade` — regenerating on every upgrade would 401 every call this
  cluster makes until each linked AI cluster refreshed its copy of the JWKS.
- **The generator cannot overwrite an identity.** Its Role grants `create` and a
  name-scoped `get`, and deliberately no `update`, `patch` or `delete`.
- **The Secret is created by `kubectl`, not Helm**, so Helm never owns it and it
  survives `helm uninstall`. That is what you want for an identity other clusters
  have been configured to trust.

P-256 is not a preference: `vg-runtime-api` pins `ES256` and rejects every other
algorithm, matching what the platform enforces for internal JWTs.

### Bringing your own key instead

Set `vgCluster.signingKey.existingSecret` and the generator Job is not rendered
at all. Generate and seal it the same way as any other cluster secret — see the
SealedSecret recipe in the repository `README.md`:

```sh
openssl ecparam -genkey -name prime256v1 -noout -out signing-key.pem
openssl ec -in signing-key.pem -pubout -out signing-key.pub.pem

kubectl create secret generic vg-cluster-signing-key \
  --namespace voicegateway \
  --from-file=signing-key.pem \
  --from-file=signing-key.pub.pem \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | kubeseal --format yaml > vg-cluster-signing-key-sealed.yaml
```

Delete the local `signing-key.pem` afterwards. Only the sealed manifest belongs
in a fleet repo.

## Helm Chart Changes

```yaml
vgCluster:
  ## Optional. Becomes the JWT `iss`, and is the key each linked AI cluster files
  ## this cluster under in its trust list. Falls back to billing.clusterId then
  ## ingress.webapp.host — the same chain api-server already uses for
  ## VG_CLUSTER_ID — so an upgraded cluster has a working identity with nothing
  ## set. Set it explicitly on a cluster you intend to link: a hostname-derived
  ## identity changes if the host does, and changing it later means editing every
  ## linked AI cluster's trust list.
  name: "vg-team-dev-thilbrich"

resourceResolver:
  ## The AI clusters this resolver may resolve against, in the order it tries
  ## them. `name` must match the key this VG cluster is filed under in the
  ## target's trust list — it becomes the JWT `aud`.
  runtimeApiTargets:
    - name: ibilousov-test
      url: https://api-ibilousov-test.cognigy.dev/vg/runtime
```

**What changes on upgrade, and what does not.** The keypair is created and
`api-server` begins serving its public half at `/.well-known/jwks.json` — where
before the endpoint returned `404`. Publishing a public key is harmless by
definition, and it is what makes linking a one-sided operation later: an AI
cluster can be pointed at this URL without anyone touching this cluster again.

Everything else stays inert. `runtimeApiTargets` is empty by default, so
`vg-resource-resolver` mounts nothing, calls nothing and presents no credential —
exactly as before. Set `vgCluster.signingKey.autoGenerate: false` to opt out of
even the keypair.

Render-time guards exist so a half-configured cluster fails loudly at reconcile
rather than quietly at call time. All of them fire **whether or not
`resourceResolver.enabled` is true** — switching the resolver off is a plausible
way to park a misbehaving link, and it must not turn a broken config into a
silent no-op:

- `runtimeApiTargets` set with no resolvable signing key (`autoGenerate: false`
  and no `existingSecret`) fails the render — the resolver would have no
  credential and every AI cluster would reject it.
- `runtimeApiTargets` set with no resolvable cluster name fails the render — an
  empty `iss` is rejected by every verifier.
- A cluster name containing whitespace fails the render. The AI side's trust list
  is keyed byte for byte, so `vg-team-dev ` is a different cluster from
  `vg-team-dev` — a 401 with nothing in it to point at the space. Case is *not*
  checked: the chart cannot know how a given AI cluster filed this one.
- A `runtimeApiTargets` entry missing `name` or `url` fails the render.

`api-server` reads its key once at boot and publishes it whenever there is one,
so it carries a `checksum/vg-cluster-signing-key` annotation and rolls when the
Secret changes. `vg-resource-resolver` carries the same annotation **only when
`runtimeApiTargets` is set** — that is when it actually mounts the key, and
annotating it merely because the Secret exists would roll the resolver fleet-wide
on the upgrade that first creates the keypair, for a feature nobody has enabled.

### Migrating off `RUNTIME_API_BASE_URL`

`runtimeApiTargets` replaces the single `RUNTIME_API_BASE_URL` (and
`RUNTIME_API_SERVICE_TOKEN`) that `vg-resource-resolver` used to read. This chart
never set either — the one place `RUNTIME_API_BASE_URL` lives today is a fleet
repo, passed through `resourceResolver.extraEnvVars`.

**Remove that `extraEnvVars` entry in the same change that sets
`runtimeApiTargets`.** The resolver no longer reads it, so a leftover is inert
rather than dangerous — but it is inert config that *looks* like it is doing the
job, and the next person to debug a link will read it and believe it. The chart
does not fail the render on it: a hard guard on a variable the consumer ignores
would block reconciles across the fleet for no operational gain.

## Verifying it worked

The failure mode this feature has is silent — cluster A's keypair sealed into
cluster B, or a `signing-key.pem` and `signing-key.pub.pem` from different
generations. Both mount fine, both boot fine, and both surface only as a 401 on
the AI side at call time. Two checks rule it out.

**1. The two halves are one pair.** Derive the public key from the mounted
private key and compare it to the mounted public key — if they match, they are a
pair, and no amount of cross-cluster mix-up survives it:

```sh
kubectl exec deploy/vg-resource-resolver -n voicegateway -- \
  openssl ec -in /var/run/secrets/vg-cluster/signing-key.pem -pubout 2>/dev/null | sha256sum
kubectl exec deploy/api-server -n voicegateway -- \
  sha256sum /var/run/secrets/vg-cluster/signing-key.pub.pem
```

(If the resolver image has no `openssl`, run the same derivation locally against
`kubectl get secret vg-cluster-signing-key -o jsonpath='{.data.signing-key\.pem}' | base64 -d`.)

**2. The JWKS endpoint serves it.** The `kid` is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the
key, so this also confirms the published key is the one being signed with:

```sh
curl -s https://<vg-webapp-host>/.well-known/jwks.json | jq
```

Expect `200` with one key, `"alg": "ES256"`, `"crv": "P-256"`, `"use": "sig"`.
The other statuses are meaningful, not generic: `404` means
`VG_CLUSTER_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH` is unset — this cluster does not participate, which
is the correct answer for an unconfigured cluster and deliberately *not* an empty
`{"keys":[]}` a verifier could not tell apart from "everything was rotated away".
`503` means the key material is mounted but unusable.

### JWKS reachability is a precondition, not a given

Publishing the key is not the same as a linked AI cluster being able to fetch it.
Two chart settings can make `/.well-known/jwks.json` unreachable while everything
above still looks correct:

- **`ingress.enabled: false`** — `templates/api-server/ingress.yaml` is wrapped in
  it, so there is no route to the endpoint at all.
- **`ingress.api.ipWhiteListMiddleware.enabled: true`** — every JWKS fetch from an
  AI cluster whose egress IPs are not on the allowlist gets a `403`.

Check both before telling an AI cluster to trust this one, and curl the URL from
outside the cluster, not just from inside it.

## Rolling back

The feature rips out cleanly, and the chart is built so that it does:

1. Unset `resourceResolver.runtimeApiTargets`. The resolver's mounts, env vars and
   checksum annotation disappear; the removed annotation is itself what rolls the
   pod, and it comes back up in exactly its pre-feature state.
2. Optionally set `vgCluster.signingKey.autoGenerate: false` to stop `api-server`
   publishing too. The endpoint returns to `404`.

**The Secret is not deleted** — it is not Helm-owned, so `helm uninstall` and a
rollback both leave it alone. Re-enabling reuses the same identity rather than
minting a new one, which is what you want: every linked AI cluster's trust list is
still keyed by it.

Signals that should trigger a rollback rather than a fix-forward: a rising 401
rate on the AI side's `vg_runtime_api_*` metrics attributed to this `iss`, or an
unexpected `iss` in an AI cluster's audit log (which means a keypair reached the
wrong cluster and is a rotation, not a rollback — see below).

## Rotating the key

`signing-key.pub.pem` may hold **several concatenated PEM blocks**, and that is
the rotation mechanism. AI clusters refresh their copy of the JWKS on a timer, so
a newly published key is not trusted everywhere the moment it appears:

1. Generate the new keypair. Append the new **public** key to
   `signing-key.pub.pem`, keeping the old one, and update the Secret.
   `api-server` rolls and now publishes both. (The generator Job does not do
   this for you — it only ever creates a keypair that is missing.)

   Verify before going on: `curl -s https://<vg-webapp-host>/.well-known/jwks.json
   | jq '.keys | length'` must return `2`.

2. **Wait longer than the AI side's refresh interval** so every linked cluster
   has seen the new `kid`. That interval is **5 minutes** — `vg-runtime-api`
   refreshes each trusted cluster's key set on a `REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS` timer of
   `5 * 60 * 1000`, matched to the `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` the JWKS
   endpoint sends. An unknown `kid` is a `401`, never a reason to fetch, so
   nothing shortens this wait. **Wait 10 minutes**, not 5: a refresh that fails
   keeps the previous key set and retries on the next tick.

   The checkpoint is on the AI side, per linked cluster, and it is not optional:

   ```sh
   # On each linked Cognigy.AI cluster — age must be well under 300, and the
   # failure gauge must be 0, for THIS cluster's issuer.
   vg_runtime_api_cluster_jwks_key_set_age_seconds{issuer="<vgCluster.name>"}
   vg_runtime_api_cluster_jwks_consecutive_failures{issuer="<vgCluster.name>"}
   ```

   A non-zero failure count means that cluster is still on the old key set and
   step 3 will 401 it. Fix the fetch before proceeding.

3. Replace `signing-key.pem` with the new private key and re-seal. The resolver
   rolls and starts signing with it; tokens verify because step 1 published the
   matching public key.
4. Wait past the token TTL (60s, bounded by the AI side's 120s `maxTokenAge`) so
   no token signed by the old key can still be in flight, then drop the old
   public key from `signing-key.pub.pem` and re-seal.

Retiring the old public key before step 2 has completed **everywhere** will 401
live traffic on every linked AI cluster that has not refreshed. The order is the
contract, not a suggestion — and step 2's checkpoint is what tells you "everywhere"
has actually happened, rather than assuming it from a clock.

`kid` is the RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint, derived from the key material itself, so
there is no id to allocate or keep in step between the two sides.
